info.title: Vertical Farm Ingestion API
info.description:
## Vertical Farm IoT Platform API

This API provides endpoints for:

- **Ingestion**: Receive sensor data from IoT devices
- **Devices**: Digital Twin device registry with real-time state
- **Capabilities**: Master definitions of what sensors can measure (units, ranges)
- **Sensor Types**: Hardware sensor definitions (DHT22, BME280) with capabilities
- **Device Capabilities**: Per-device calibration and configuration
- **Thresholds**: Per-device alerting thresholds
- **Alerts**: Webhook-based alerting system

### Authentication

All endpoints require the `X-Farm-Key` header with a valid API key.

### Capabilities Architecture

```
capabilities (master definitions)
     ↑
sensor_types (hardware models with accuracy specs)
     ↑
devices (linked to sensor_type, with calibration overrides)
```

get.description:
List all roles with their permissions.

**Deliberately NOT farm-scoped** (GAP-AUTH-01, task 10). `roles` is a
platform-wide catalogue of role definitions — five seeded system rows
(`superadmin`, `owner`, `admin`, `operator`, `viewer`) plus any custom
role created through `POST /roles` — and it is not tenant data. The
table has no `farm_id` and no `org_id` column, and there is nothing to
give it one from: a role is a name attached to a set of permission
strings, identical for every tenant. A farm filter here would not
restrict a disclosure, it would just hide the vocabulary the caller
needs to read their own `user_roles`/`user_orgs` rows.

So this is an intentional open catalogue, in the same category as
`GET /api/v1/sensor-types` and `GET /api/v1/capabilities` (main.py) —
both likewise farm-less reference tables served unscoped on purpose.
`/roles` is deliberately absent from `LIST_ROUTES` in
`tests/e2e/test_40_farm_scope_sweep.py` for this reason; do not add it.

Be honest about the `require_permission` call below: it is **not** a
gate. Called without a `farm_id` it returns early for every JWT
(`auth_middleware.py`, resolution step 3), so in practice any
authenticated caller reads the catalogue regardless of whether they
hold `roles:read` — verified against this deployment: a freshly
registered zero-grant user gets 200 and all five rows. That is the same
early return that made `/users` leak, and it is left in place here
only because the catalogue is open by design; it is not evidence that
a permission check is happening. Don't copy this shape to a route that
returns tenant rows.

get.description:
List users with their farm role assignments, scoped to the caller's farms.

GAP-AUTH-01 **cause (b)**. Unlike the routes fixed in tasks 5-7, this
one was never missing its `require_permission` call — the call below
has always been here. It is simply not a scope check: with no
`farm_id` argument `require_permission` returns early for every JWT
("endpoint should handle farm scoping itself", `auth_middleware.py`
resolution step 3), and no endpoint ever did. A freshly registered
zero-grant user therefore read the whole directory: 50 rows and
`total: 133` on this deployment. The call is kept — it still gates
API-key/JWT authentication shape and stays correct if the resolution
order ever changes — and the scoping is added alongside it.

get.description:
List all farms.

Farms are the top-level grouping for devices. Each farm has a unique ID
and contains devices at various rack/node/position locations.

post.description:
Grant operator/viewer on N farms in one atomic call.

Validation order:
  1. Pydantic: role_id ∈ {operator, viewer}, farm_ids non-empty, ≤100.
  2. All farm_ids exist + share one org (resolve_org_for_farms).
  3. Caller is superadmin OR org-admin on that org.
  4. Target user exists + is active.
  5. INSERT all rows in one transaction (ON CONFLICT upgrades role).

Atomicity: any failure rolls back zero changes. UI doesn't have to
reconcile a partial 3-of-5-succeeded state.

delete.description:
Atomic counterpart to /farms/grants POST. Returns the grants
that were actually deleted (may be < len(farm_ids) when the user
didn't have a row on some — that's a no-op, not an error).

- Org-admin: rows only for farms in orgs the caller admins.
- Other JWT: rows only for farms where the caller has any role

The whole physical picture of a farm in one read. Same guard as
the zone list: a per-farm X-Farm-Key may read it.

Loads (lights/fans/motors) placed at the given target and not yet
attached to any relay — the list the relay page's "Attach actuator" form
offers. `zone_id` is required; add `location_id`/`sublocation_id` to match a
deeper target exactly. Same read authorization as the zone list.

delete.description:
Retires (is_active = false); it does not delete.

The device FK is NO ACTION, so a hard delete of an occupied zone
would surface as a constraint violation. Idempotent — retiring twice
is 204. Children are NOT retired with it; the DB cascade is on
DELETE, which this API never issues.

get.description:
List organizations.

- **Superadmin**: every org in the system.
- **Anyone else**: only orgs the caller has a `user_orgs` membership in.

The result list is unioned with member-only filtering; pagination is
applied after filtering. `is_active=false` lets superadmin see
soft-deleted orgs.

post.description:
Create a new organization. Superadmin only.

The creator is auto-granted `admin` on the new org so they don't
have to mint themselves into it via a separate call. This mirrors
the pattern in `main.py:3750` for farms (since removed in Phase D
— admin lives in user_orgs now, not user_roles).

get.description:
Get one organization. 404 if the caller is not a member and not
superadmin (don't leak existence via 403).

patch.description:
Update org metadata. Superadmin OR org admin on this org.

Slug is not updatable — see OrgUpdate docstring.

delete.description:
Soft-delete an organization. Superadmin only.

Refuses (409) if any active farms still belong to this org — the
superadmin must explicitly detach them first. The FK is
ON DELETE SET NULL, so a hard delete would silently orphan farms;
we don't trust callers to know that's what they want.

get.description:
List farms attached to this org. Per-farm `device_count` is
computed in one batch query (same pattern as `GET /farms`).

schema.title: Response List Organization Farms Api V1 Organizations  Org Id  Farms Get

get.description:
Device inventory allocated to this organisation.

Org admin only, or superadmin. This is the module's one admin-gated
read — `_require_org_admin`'s docstring says reads accept any
membership — because the view was asked for specifically for admins.
Widening it is a one-line change to `_can_read_org`. Note that today
the distinction is academic: `OrgMemberGrantRequest.role_id` is
regex-locked to `^admin$`, so every org member IS an admin.

404 rather than 403 for a non-admin, matching the read-side
existence-leak guard used by the sibling endpoints.

Unlike the superadmin list there is no implicit `status <> 'retired'`
filter — an admin asking "where did that unit go" should get an
answer rather than silence.

post.description:
Register a kiosk onto one of this org's farms and issue a pairing PIN.

Org admin only, JWT only — an API key must never mint another
credential.

The PIN returned here is not the kiosk's credential. It is typed in
once at the kiosk and exchanged at POST /api/v1/kiosks/pair for a
long-lived passkey.

get.description:
Re-read the live pairing PIN.

This endpoint is why PINs are encrypted rather than hashed: without
it, an admin who closed the modal has stranded the kiosk.

post.description: Issue a fresh pairing PIN, invalidating any live one.

get.description:
Where this kiosk stands: paired, connected, or arguing with us.

Every field is a projection of tables the caller can already read
through existing endpoints. This exists to do the join server-side and
once, so the two UIs cannot each derive a different answer — the bug
this whole design starts from is exactly that kind of drift.

Here rather than in kiosk_routes.py: that module is the
unauthenticated device-facing surface, rate-limited as a unit, and its
docstring makes that a deliberate boundary. This is an operator
endpoint behind a JWT and belongs with its /pin and /passkey siblings.

Note this deliberately does NOT return the pairing PIN — only whether
one is live. GET .../pin stays the single way to read it.

Report whether this kiosk holds a credential, and its state.

Never returns the passkey — it is shown once by the pairing call and
stored only as a hash. This answers "is this wall authorised", which the
tokens page can no longer answer since kiosk credentials moved to their
own table (migration d4c3b2a1f0e9).

delete.description:
Cut a kiosk's access immediately.

The remote kill switch for a lost or stolen wall display. Before kiosk
credentials moved to their own table an admin could do this from the
tokens page; token_routes revokes through farm_api_keys, which no longer
holds the live row, so without this endpoint the only remaining option
would be re-pairing — which needs a human standing at the device, exactly
what you cannot do with a unit that has walked off.

Idempotent: revoking an already-revoked kiosk returns revoked=0 rather
than an error.

The kiosk is NOT unpaired by this. Its serial and bootstrap key are
untouched, so it can be brought back with a fresh PIN once recovered.

get.description: List members of this org with their org-scoped role.

schema.title: Response List Organization Members Api V1 Organizations  Org Id  Users Get

post.description:
Attach an existing farm to this org. Superadmin only.

Org-admins do NOT move their own farms — they create new ones in
their org via POST /farms (which auto-attaches). Moving a farm
between orgs is a platform-level concern (billing/audit) and
deliberately requires superadmin.

delete.description:
Detach a farm from this org. Superadmin only.

The org-admin would lose access to the farm after detach — which
is exactly why an org-admin can't do this to themselves. Only
superadmin can detach.

post.description:
Grant an org-scoped role to a user.

Body's `role_id` is currently restricted to `admin` (Pydantic
enforced) — operator/viewer remain farm-scoped via
POST /api/v1/farms/grants. The validator is the only gate until
Phase E's DB CHECK constraint ships.

delete.description:
Remove an org member. Refuses (409) if it would leave the org
with zero admins.

A superadmin removing themselves from their own grant doesn't
leave the org admin-less because superadmin acts platform-wide
without needing a user_orgs row — but for safety we still apply
the guard uniformly. If you really want zero admins, soft-delete
the org instead.

post.description:
Issue a new per-farm API key.

Auth: JWT only — an API key cannot mint another key (a leaked
gateway key must not be able to escalate itself). Caller needs
`farms:manage` on `body.farm_id`.

`expires_at` is the admin-picked DD/MM/YYYY date; we convert it
to a UTC end-of-day datetime and reject anything ≤ now. `null`
means "never expires".

get.summary: List tokens visible to the caller
get.description:
List per-farm tokens the caller is allowed to see.

Visibility rule (enforced server-side): a row appears only if the
caller has any of `farms:read` / `farms:manage` / `farms:*` /
`*:*` on the token's farm. Superadmins see every row. Never trust
a client-supplied `farm_id` to override the filter.

Query params:
  `farm_id` — narrow to one farm (still subject to visibility).
  `status` — filter by derived status; one of active, expiring_soon,
             in_grace, expired, revoked.
  `include_revoked` — default false (`revoked_at IS NOT NULL` rows
                      are hidden unless asked for).
  `lead_hours` — when combined with `status=expiring_soon`,
                 narrows the window further to rows whose
                 `expires_at <= NOW() + lead_hours`. Task 27 —
                 the standalone key-rotator uses this with
                 `lead_hours=48` to find keys due for auto-rotation
                 without re-implementing the validity SQL.

get.summary: Fetch a single token's metadata (never returns raw_key)
get.description:
Fetch a token by id. Caller needs visibility on the token's
farm (`farms:read` / `farms:manage` / wildcard, or superadmin).

404 covers two cases: the id doesn't exist, AND the caller has no
visibility on that farm. Returning 403 in the latter would leak
the row's existence to an unauthorised caller.

delete.description:
Soft-revoke a token. The next auth attempt with the raw key
returns 401 immediately (no TTL wait — Phase C also drops it
from the Redis cache).

Auth: JWT only (an API key cannot revoke another key — would
let a leaked gateway key kill its peers). Caller needs
`farms:manage` on the token's farm.

Status codes:
  204 — revoked.
  404 — token not found.
  403 — caller lacks `farms:manage` on the token's farm.
  410 — token is already revoked (idempotent-safe).

post.summary: Rotate a token, leaving the predecessor in a grace window
post.description:
Issue a successor for an existing token.

Both keys stay valid until `grace_period_ends_at` on the
predecessor — this is the window the Pi has to swap its config.
The new raw key is returned exactly once.

Auth: JWT only (an API key cannot rotate another key — would let
a leaked gateway key escalate itself). Caller needs
`farms:manage` on the token's farm.

Status codes:
  201 — successor issued.
  404 — token not found.
  403 — caller lacks `farms:manage` on the token's farm.
  409 — token is already revoked, or already in a grace window
        (chained rotations not allowed; revoke + new instead).
Answer a natural-language question about one device's recent sensor data.

for the life of the hardware, and ON DELETE RESTRICT would refuse a
hard delete anyway. Reactivate with PATCH {"is_active": true}.

delete.description:
Deactivate, never drop — inventory rows reference this for the
life of the hardware. Refuses while non-retired stock exists so the
ON DELETE RESTRICT never surfaces as a psycopg2 500.

Retire, never drop. A serial records a physical object that was
purchased; hard deletion loses the audit trail and a later re-add of
the same serial would look like a new unit.

post.description:
Re-issue a unit's bootstrap key, invalidating the previous one.

Needed for the re-work cases in the burn-in runbook (M7): a mistyped
serial, a suspected key exposure, a unit whose provisioning was never
completed. Overwriting the hash IS the revocation — there is no separate
revoked flag, so there is nothing that can drift out of step with it.

Superadmin JWT only, via the same _guard as every other route here.

Apply a config to a cabinet: one append-only unit_configs row.

Checks in order, first refusal wins, nothing written until all pass:
serial known → cabinet and allocated → hash known → not already
current → later than the current row. The INSERT re-checks both
"later" and "not already current" against the DB's own now() and own
current row in the same statement, so a future-dated row cannot be
overtaken by a default-timestamp apply, and two simultaneous applies
of the current hash — both of which pass the pre-check's 409 read —
cannot both insert: the loser's INSERT is skipped by the WHERE clause
and the post-miss lookup turns that into the same 409, not a bogus 422.
Hand a stocked unit to a customer organisation.
Take an allocated unit back into general stock.

Exchange a 6-digit pairing PIN for a long-lived passkey.

Two factors, checked in this order and never the reverse:

  1. AUTHENTICATE — X-Bootstrap-Key, burned into this unit at
     manufacture and stored SHA-256 against its serial. This proves the
     caller is the device.
  2. VERIFY — the PIN, which proves an admin registered this device to a
     farm. Single use, 24h, burns after MAX_PIN_ATTEMPTS.

The order is the point. A caller without the bootstrap key never reaches
the PIN row, so it cannot advance the attempt counter — otherwise anyone
who could read a serial off the case could burn that kiosk's live PIN
with five wrong guesses and keep the unit unpairable.

Still unauthenticated in the verify_auth sense: the kiosk holds no JWT
and no passkey. The bootstrap key is checked here explicitly rather than
through the middleware, which knows only about those two credentials.

Which rungs a device of this type may be attached at.

An EMPTY list is a real answer — "nowhere yet" — which is why an

The whole matrix in one call.

One request, because the UI needs every type's rules to grey out a

Families are returned alongside: a device with no model is judged on

Upsert, so re-declaring adjusts the row rather than 409ing. Declaring is
idempotent by nature — the caller is stating a fact, not creating an object.

Soft delete. Refused while any device type or device model still
declares/measures the property — deleting it out from under them would
leave the ladder pointing at nothing.

get.description:
What is attached to this device, and what each attached device reads.

Directly attached children only. A device with nothing attached returns an
empty list, not a 404 — "nothing is attached" is an answer, not an error.

get.description:
No `require_permission`: the spec gives this route exactly the read
access of GET /frames/{image_id}, which scopes by farm and nothing else.

Cache headers match the legacy image route: a frame's bytes never change
for its id, and the response is private because it is farm-scoped.

schema.description: The image_id returned by POST /api/v1/vision/images (a frame's id is its image's id).
schema.title: Image Id

parameters.description: The image_id returned by POST /api/v1/vision/images (a frame's id is its image's id).

get.summary: A random sample of frames to put in the eval pool
get.description:
Two identical-answer guarantees, in order:

A per-farm API key gets 403 for any farm that is not its own, whether
or not that farm even exists — `require_api_key_farm_match` runs on
the RAW `farm_id` first and canonicalises both sides itself, so it
never leaks which farm codes are real to a key scoped elsewhere.

A JWT (or global-key) caller skips that check and instead gets one
identical 404 for an unknown farm and a farm outside their scope:
resolve, then scope, then permission.

post.summary: Ingest a plant image: store it and queue its analysis
post.description:
The one ingest. Stores the frame at the readable key `build_key`
produces, writes the gallery row, the engine's frame row (with crop and
place) and its job in ONE transaction, then queues the analysis with a
metadata snapshot on the stream. Always analyses; the pipeline is
controlled per crop, not per call.

`image_id` is the idempotency key. Omit it and the server mints one —
convenient for a human on Swagger, but every retry then becomes a new
image, so anything automated sends its own. `crop` is recorded
verbatim; an unknown crop runs the generic pipeline rather than being
refused — a capture the operator cannot retake is evidence.

get.description:
Images taken in a place, newest first, filtered by STAMPED placement.

Filters are independent and inclusive of deeper rungs: `zone_id` alone
returns everything stamped with that zone, including frames also stamped
with a location and a tray beneath it. This is a FILTER, not the
exact-rung rule that aggregation uses — no aggregation happens here, and
the narrower rule would only surprise.

An unplaced camera's frames carry NULL placement and therefore belong to
no place: they are returned only by an unfiltered query.

`verdict` is now real, sourced from `vision_verdicts` via
`get_verdicts_for_frames` and projected through the same `summarise()`
that `/images/{id}/analysis` uses — not the constant-null placeholder
this route used to return. `stages_run`/`stages_ok` are always `0` here
regardless of what the frame's verdicts say: that count is a per-frame
`vision_derivations` query, and a page of up to 500 frames does not pay
for 500 of them. Poll `/images/{id}/analysis` for the real counts.

get.summary: Mint a URL for a stored plant image
get.description: Return a URL the UI can put straight into . For S3-backed rows this is a short-lived presigned URL, so the bytes travel S3 -> browser and never through this process. Farm-scoped at mint time: once minted, possession of the URL is read access until it expires, which is why the TTL is short and why the URL is never logged. A batch variant (POST /images/urls taking {image_ids: [...]}) is the intended shape if a gallery view ever needs it — one query with `WHERE image_id = ANY(...)`, one farm check per row, N local signatures. Not built: minting is cheap enough that N calls are fine today.

Stream a stored image back, scoped to the owning farm. Serves from S3
when `blob_key` is an S3 key, else falls back to the filesystem.
Auth-gated — never a public static mount.

get.summary: Where and when an image was taken
get.description:
The image's place, as STAMPED AT CAPTURE — not where the camera is now.

`/images/{image_id}` streams the bytes; this returns the facts about them.
All three rungs are always present as keys; any may be null, meaning the
camera was not placed at that rung when the frame was taken.

patch.description:
Upserts: PATCHing a camera that has no schedule creates one.

Changing `interval_minutes` recomputes `next_due_at` from `last_fired_at`,
so a shortened interval takes effect immediately.

get.description:
Properties measured by the devices attached at or below this place.

CONTAINMENT, like everything else here: a devices row carries its full
path, so filtering on zone_id reaches a tray-attached device too.

An EMPTY list is a real answer — "nothing here measures anything yet"
— and the caller must render it differently from a failure. That is
exactly why the farm this place belongs to is resolved from the
place's OWN table (`_place_farm_id`), never through `devices`: a
place with nothing attached still belongs to a farm, and resolving
through devices would 404 the empty case this docstring calls real.

A place outside the caller's scope 404s byte-identically to an
unknown place id (`_PLACE_NOT_FOUND`), so the response cannot be used
to confirm a place exists on a farm/org the caller has no grant on.

parameters.name: since

schema.description: ISO 8601 timestamp; only events with fired_at >= since
schema.title: Since

parameters.description: ISO 8601 timestamp; only events with fired_at >= since

get.description:
Alerts currently open, optionally narrowed to a place.

NEW SURFACE, not a new filter on an old one. alerts.alert_state was
reachable only through the kiosk WebSocket, so nothing outside the
kiosk could list live alerts at all.

A place filter is CONTAINMENT: `zone_id` returns every open alert
beneath that zone, including devices attached at location and
sub-location level.

Farm scoping (alerts-read-scoping, task 1): `scope_condition` with a
hardcoded literal column — `"a.farm_id"`, the alias `_OPEN_FROM` uses
for `alerts.alert_state` — restricts a JWT caller to their own
farms. API keys and superadmins get (None, {}) and run unfiltered,
exactly as today (GAP-AUTH-03; not this project's scope).

post.description:
Close an open alert because a human looked at it.

Spec SS8.3: a vision verdict requires human acknowledgement, and the
machine that raised the finding must not be able to retract it. One
clean frame does not mean the tipburn is gone -- it may mean a bad
angle.

Nothing here is vision-specific: a threshold alert acknowledges the
same way, which is why the route lives with the alerts routes rather
than in the vision package.

Auth: JWT only. `require_permission` alone is NOT enough here --
it explicitly bypasses ALL permission checks for
`auth_type == "api_key"` ("full access for devices" is its general
contract). An X-Farm-Key would sail straight through it if that were
the only gate. `require_jwt` is what actually keeps acknowledgement a
human act, mirroring the existing "API keys cannot mint other API
keys" rule on the token routes.

This is no longer unique to this route (alerts-tenant-boundary, task
2): rule management (`create_rule`, `update_rule`, `delete_rule`,
`fire_test`) is JWT-only too, via `dependencies=[Depends(require_jwt)]`
on each decorator rather than a call in the body -- FastAPI runs a
route dependency before the body executes, so ordering does not need
a comment defending it there the way it does for this route's inline
call.

`require_jwt` runs FIRST, before any row is even read (round-1
review finding C1). `accessible_farm_ids` returns `ALL_FARMS` for
`auth_type == "api_key"`, so `assert_in_scope` never rejects a
device key -- placed after the read, a farm key got 404 for an
unknown id and 403 for a real one, an existence oracle over
`alerts.alert_state` handed to the least-trusted credential in the
system. Rejecting the auth type before touching the database makes
both responses identical, and is also cheaper: no DB read on behalf
of a caller who was never going to be allowed past it.

get.description:
Open-alert counts per place at one rung.

CONTAINMENT: the same alert appears at every rung above its device.
That is not double counting — each rung answers a different question
— but CALLERS MUST NOT SUM ACROSS RUNGS.

An empty list means NO DEVICE IS ATTACHED AT THIS RUNG, not that
everything is fine. Render it as "no sensors at this level"; a zero
or a tick would say the opposite of the truth.

Farm scoping (alerts-read-scoping, task 2): `scope_condition` with a
hardcoded literal column — `"a.farm_id"`, the alias `_OPEN_FROM`
uses for `alerts.alert_state` — restricts a JWT caller to their own
farms, including when a foreign `farm_id` is supplied explicitly:
the scope clause and the `farm_id` filter both land in the same
`where` list, so a foreign id simply matches nothing rather than
bypassing the restriction. API keys and superadmins get (None, {})
and run unfiltered, exactly as today (GAP-AUTH-03; not this
project's scope). The containment predicate is unchanged.

post.description:
Synthetic firing.

By default this records an `alert_events` row and stops — no POST. That
is deliberate and pinned by test_fire_records_no_delivery; the e2e
fixtures point at httpbin and a dead port, so delivering by default
would make every test-fire either hit the internet or burn ~12 s in
retries.

`?deliver=true` sends it down the real path instead — envelope,
receiver registry, renderer — so the row carries a real
webhook_status. That is what the user-ui drawer's "Send test" uses,
and what a runbook needs to confirm a receiver is actually reachable.

NO fixed fields. `temperature` and `humidity` used to be declared and

reporting only its WiFi signal, a pH probe reporting only pH — could
not post at all. What a device may report is decided by the
properties its device model declares, checked in main.py against
device_model_properties. This model's only job is to carry them.

new_expires_at.title: New Expires At
new_expires_at.description: Override the successor's expires_at (ISO-8601 UTC). Omit to inherit the predecessor's value. Must be in the future and ≥ predecessor.expires_at when set.

RotateTokenRequest.title: RotateTokenRequest
RotateTokenRequest.description:
Body for POST /api/v1/tokens/{id}/rotate.

`grace_hours` controls how long the predecessor key keeps working
after the successor is issued — gives the Pi a window to swap
config without coordinating downtime. Bounds: 1 hour to 7 days.

`new_expires_at` is the auto-rotation hook (task 27). When omitted
(manual UI flow), the successor inherits the predecessor's
`expires_at` — same behaviour the route has always had. When set
(standalone key-rotator), the successor uses this override so the
rotator can avoid the self-sustaining trap where a successor
inheriting expires_at would immediately re-enter its own rotation
window.

Format is ISO-8601 UTC (e.g. `"2026-09-01T00:00:00+00:00"`) — chosen
over the DD/MM/YYYY humans use in `CreateTokenRequest` because the
rotator is a machine client and `datetime.isoformat()` emits this
naturally. Naive datetimes (no timezone) are rejected: we want
explicit intent, not silent UTC coercion.

two counts are 0 when the image has no frame.
